extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy; educated laypersons, statesmen, or critics interested in evaluating forms of government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and standards for judging political constitutions (despotism, aristocracy, democracy, mixed government) as argued in a political-philosophical essay. Focuses on practical consequences, stability, corruption, and the effects of institutions on morals and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism: concentration of sovereign will
rubrics_metrics.description: Government 'where all the inferior orbs of power are moved merely by the will of the Supreme' — a single supreme will directs all offices and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate despotism by its central features and consequences: extreme caprice in rule, the ruler's pleasures increasing as subjects' misery increases, systemic corruption of heart and understanding, prevalence of flatterers and court philosophers who justify any act (e.g., 'that let a sovereign do what he wilt, all his actions are just and lawful'), arbitrary punishments (slight displeasure may be death), and the tendency toward debauchery, murder, and horrid outrages (historical examples: Nero, Alexander).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy as de facto despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy in which the many are excluded from legislative power is effectively as much a slavery as rule by one: 'a people who are in general excluded from any share of the legislative, are, to all intents and purposes, as much slaves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge aristocracies by how exclusion of the majority produces pride, suspicion, immutable maxims, and a concealed despotism: rulers preserve authority, share vices of a despot (haughtiness, oppression), corrode public virtue through luxury and debauchery, and make the people worse off—often more intolerable than open despotism (Venice and Genoa as examples). Consider also that aristocratic bodies resist reform and rarely soften over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy: vulnerability to demagogues and tyranny of the many
rubrics_metrics.description: When the people transact public business in their own persons, an 'artful man' can become popular and convert popular power into oppression and slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess democracies for susceptibility to charismatic demagogues, factionalism, bribed orators, and collective passions that lead to injustice: banishment, persecution of merit (ostracism), wasteful public expenditure and extravagance, rash wars, and the transformation of civic virtue into vice (example: Athens — five thousand deprived and sold as slaves; banishment of Themistocles, exile of Aristides, poisoning of Socrates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government: complexity breeds instability
rubrics_metrics.description: The junction of regal, aristocratic, and popular powers forms 'a very complex, nice, and intricate machine' which is liable to disorder from many accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mixed systems for the practical risks introduced by structural complexity: frequent cabals, tumults, revolutions; contests over which part has which function; persistent party struggles; and long-running indeterminacy that diverts attention from governing to internal power contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party spirit as a corrosive force
rubrics_metrics.description: Party is 'the great instrument of all these changes' and is driven by 'the spirit of ambition, of self-interest, of oppression and treachery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure political systems by the extent to which party affiliation drives decisions rather than merit or justice: decisions resolved by party advantage, reversal of principles, betrayal of public safety, and the erosion of honesty and equal justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indeterminacy of rights and functions causes abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Where constituent parts have 'distinct rights' that are 'so indeterminate in their nature' disputes over functions create constant debate and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge institutions on clarity of jurisdiction and rights: indeterminate powers produce endless contests over office and functions, stall government business, permit fraud and impunity to grow into customary abuse, and ultimately make abuses too inveterate to cure without violent remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical consequences over speculative planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique political schemes by their real, known consequences rather than by what 'seems most eligible to their imaginations': 'I discover the mistakes in those plans, from the real known consequences which have resulted from them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating constitutions or reforms, prioritize historical examples and observable effects over idealized theory. Avoid defending arrangements merely because they seem elegant in imagination; demand evidence of actual outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custodial problem: who guards the governors?
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when power is entrusted to others to guard against men's passions, a worse difficulty arises: 'how to be defended against the governors? Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess any delegation of authority for checks and controls: protect against governors' own passions and propensity to unite for self-gratification; recognize that shifting from one ruler to a few does not eliminate the problem but reconstitutes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of institutions on popular character and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Political systems shape popular character: under oppression 'the gross of the people... are considered as a mere herd of cattle' and 'all principle of honest pride... is lost in their slavery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate governments by their impact on citizens' moral and psychological condition: whether they preserve dignity, prompt action and public spirit, or degrade people into fear, apathy, debauchery, and loss of reasoned capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability trade-offs: caprice vs rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A despot's caprice may produce good or bad rulers in succession ('a despotism... may, by the same caprice otherwise exerted, be as lovely the next'), whereas an aristocracy 'never changes its maxims' and is uniformly rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh institutions by trade-offs between chance-based variability (possible occasional good rulers under despotism) and systemic permanence (entrenched aristocratic vices). Consider whether occasional good rule offsets systemic oppression or whether rigidity makes reform impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual breadth of freedom: proportion and duration matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling a state 'free' is misleading if the free constitute a very small fraction: e.g., Athens' freemen compared to hundreds of thousands of slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of freedom by looking at who truly enjoys rights (numerical proportion of free citizens) and the temporal extent of that freedom; small, transient exceptions do not justify a positive judgment about 'society' at large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of flatterers and court culture in corrupting rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers are 'surrounded by a crowd of infamous flatterers' who keep them 'from the least light of reason' and thus accelerate corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the informational and cultural environment around leaders: presence of 'courtly philosophers' who justify all acts, flatterers who insulate rulers from criticism, and institutional tendencies that remove shame/fear and thereby enable worse conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proliferation of laws and commentary yields uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to replace discretionary judges with laws lead to multiplication of words, notes, glosses, reports, and competing authorities, bringing 'confusion' and an 'Egyptian darkness' to practical certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge legal and institutional reforms by their downstream effects on clarity and litigation: more laws and interpretive authorities may increase conflicts, delay justice, and make inheritances and rights prizes for disputation rather than secure possessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of forms preserves vices of each component
rubrics_metrics.description: Even united, the parts of a mixed government 'preserve the spirit which each form has separately' (kings ambitious, nobility haughty, populace tumultuous), so mixing does not eliminate underlying faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating hybrid constitutions, check whether combining elements actually mitigates their defects or simply aggregates the worst tendencies (perpetual party contests, contests over prerogative, and combination of abuses).
